# How to use this guide

Advanced Biopharmaceutics and Pharmacokinetics (MPH202T) is a numerical, concept-heavy postgraduate paper. Study one unit at a time: read the notes, redo every worked example with a calculator without looking, draw each graph once from memory (hysteresis loop, two-compartment curve, Michaelis–Menten curve, BE crossover scheme), then answer the question bank. Each unit has very short (2-mark), short (5-mark) and long (10-mark) questions, rated by how likely that kind of question is.

**How the units map to the PCI syllabus.** The PCI syllabus has five units. Syllabus Unit 3 is very large, so it is split here: Unit 3 covers compartmental and non-compartmental pharmacokinetics, and Unit 4 covers nonlinear pharmacokinetics and drug interactions. Syllabus Units 4 and 5 appear here as Units 5 and 6.

| Here | PCI syllabus | Content |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit 1 | Unit 1 | GI absorption, pH-partition, dissolution, dosage forms, transport model, solubility and permeability methods |
| Unit 2 | Unit 2 | Product design, dissolution testing, IVIVC, f1/f2, stability |
| Unit 3 | Unit 3 (first half) | One- and two-compartment models, Wagner–Nelson, non-compartmental analysis |
| Unit 4 | Unit 3 (second half) | Nonlinear kinetics, Km and Vmax, protein/tissue binding, CYP and transporter interactions |
| Unit 5 | Unit 4 | BA/BE design and statistics, review process, BCS, biosimilars, generic substitution |
| Unit 6 | Unit 5 | PK/PD, modified-release and targeted systems, biotech drugs |

**Worked examples.** All data tables use example numbers for hypothetical drugs, chosen so that the arithmetic is clear. They are not values for any real medicine. The same "Drug X" used in the B.Pharm course (KE 0.1733 h⁻¹, t½ 4 h, Vd 25 L, CL 4.33 L/h, F 0.8, Ka 1.2 h⁻¹) runs through Units 3, 5 and 6, so you can see how compartmental, non-compartmental, bioavailability and extended-release calculations fit together. "Drug Y" shows the two-compartment model and "Drug Z" capacity-limited elimination.

**End-semester paper (75 marks, 3 hours).** The PCI M.Pharm scheme gives MPH202T 100 marks: 25 internal assessment and 75 in the end-semester theory examination of 3 hours. PCI does not set a question pattern for M.Pharm, so the mock paper here uses the common PCI 75-mark split (also used for M.Pharm by some universities, for example Bahra University, Shimla). Confirm the exact pattern with your university.

| Section | What it asks | Marks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Objective / MCQ | 20 × 1 = 20 |
| B | Long answers — attempt 2 of 3 | 2 × 10 = 20 |
| C | Short answers — attempt 7 of 9 | 7 × 5 = 35 |

**Probability ratings**

- **High** — a central topic that appears in most papers; prepare the full answer with equations, a graph and a worked numerical.
- **Medium** — appears every few years or as part of a bigger question.
- **Low** — less common, but useful for MCQs and as a backup choice.

These ratings are estimates from syllabus weight and common patterns in pharmacokinetics papers. They are not a promise of what will be asked.

**Where the marks usually come from**

| Unit | Topics that keep coming back |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | pH-partition theory and its limitations, Noyes–Whitney and factors affecting dissolution, dosage-form effects, Caco-2 and perfusion methods, tight junctions and microclimate pH |
| 2 | Compendial dissolution apparatus, IVIVC levels and validation, f1/f2 numericals, rate-limiting steps, design of a drug product |
| 3 | Two-compartment parameters, Wagner–Nelson, statistical moments (MRT, MAT), compartment vs non-compartment approaches |
| 4 | Causes of nonlinearity, Michaelis–Menten numericals (Km, Vmax, Css), protein-binding displacement, CYP inhibition and induction, transporters |
| 5 | BE study design, 90% CI and TOST, BCS and biowaivers, biosimilars, special concerns, generic substitution |
| 6 | PK/PD models and hysteresis, extended-release design numerical, targeting index, PK of monoclonal antibodies and oligonucleotides |

**Scoring tips for this subject**

1. Begin every derivation with the model diagram and assumptions, then the differential equation, its solution, and the meaning of each symbol with units.
2. Numericals: write the formula, substitute with units, give the answer with units (mg/L, L/h, h⁻¹, mg·h/L). Method marks are given even if the arithmetic slips; a sense check (for example V1 < Vss < Vβ, GMR inside its CI) earns credit.
3. Draw the right graph: semilog plot with residuals, Michaelis–Menten rate curve, AUC vs dose curves for nonlinearity, effect vs concentration loop, BE confidence-interval diagram with 80 and 125% lines.
4. In BE answers always state the regulatory numbers: 90% CI, 80.00–125.00%, log-transformed AUC and Cmax, washout ≥ 5 half-lives, sampling ≥ 3 half-lives, NTI 90.00–111.11%.
5. For drug interactions, name the mechanism (enzyme or transporter), the direction (inhibition or induction), the time course, and a mechanistic example; add the AUC-ratio equation for extra marks.
6. Link biopharmaceutics to regulation: ICH M9 (BCS biowaivers), ICH M10 (bioanalysis), ICH M12 (drug interactions), ICH Q1A (stability), CDSCO and the New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019.
7. Postgraduate examiners reward recent concepts: transport model (1/Peff = 1/PABL + 1/(Pm + Ppara)), TMDD, FcRn recycling, GalNAc conjugates, reference-scaled BE for highly variable drugs.

# Last-night revision sheet

## Unit 1 — GI absorption

- Rate-limiting: dissolution (poorly soluble) or permeation (poorly permeable). F = fa × FG × FH.
- % un-ionised: acid 100/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)); base 100/(1 + 10^(pKa − pH)). Ion trapping ratio for acid = (1 + 10^(pHp − pKa))/(1 + 10^(pHg − pKa)).
- pH-partition limits: intestinal surface area, microclimate pH (5.5–6.5), unstirred layer, ionised species cross, carriers, dissolution ignored.
- Noyes–Whitney: dM/dt = DA(Cs − C)/h. Hixson–Crowell: W0^(1/3) − W^(1/3) = κt.
- Dosage form order: solution > suspension > capsule > tablet > coated tablet.
- Transport model: 1/Peff = 1/PABL + 1/(Pm + Ppara); Pm = P0 × fneutral; flux = Peff × Cs. MAD = S × Ka × 250 mL × 270 min.
- Tight junctions: claudins, occludin, ZO; favour small hydrophilic cations. Intracellular pH 7.0–7.2.
- Permeability: PAMPA, Caco-2 (Papp = (dQ/dt)/(A C0); efflux ratio ≥ 2), MDCK-MDR1, Ussing chamber, everted sac, SPIP Peff = −Q ln(Cout/Cin)/(2πrL), Loc-I-Gut.

## Unit 2 — Product design and in vitro performance

- D0 = (dose/250)/Cs; IDR > 1 mg/min/cm² rarely limiting, < 0.1 problematic.
- USP apparatus 1–7: basket, paddle, reciprocating cylinder, flow-through, paddle over disc, rotating cylinder, reciprocating holder. 37 ± 0.5 °C, 900 mL, pH 1.2/4.5/6.8, sink ≥ 3 × saturation volume.
- S1 each ≥ Q + 5%; S2 mean(12) ≥ Q, none < Q − 15%; S3 mean(24) ≥ Q, ≤ 2 < Q − 15%, none < Q − 25%.
- IVIVC A (point-to-point) > B (MDT vs MRT) > C (single point); %PE ≤ 10% mean, ≤ 15% each.
- f1 = Σ|R − T|/ΣR × 100 (0–15); f2 = 50 log{[1 + Σ(R − T)²/n]^(−0.5) × 100} (50–100). Example: f1 8.9, f2 61.3.
- MDT = Σ tmid ΔM/Σ ΔM; DE = area/(100 × t). Korsmeyer–Peppas n (slab): 0.5 Fickian, 1 Case II.
- India zone IVb: 30 °C/75% RH long term; 40 °C/75% RH accelerated.

## Unit 3 — Compartment and NCA

- IV bolus: C = C0 e^(−Kt); Vd = X0/C0; AUC = C0/K; CL = KVd.
- Infusion: Css = R0/CL; 90% in 3.32 t½; DL = Css Vd.
- Oral: tmax = ln(Ka/K)/(Ka − K); AUC = F X0/CL; flip-flop if Ka < K.
- Wagner–Nelson: FA = (C + K·AUC0–t)/(K·AUC0–∞). Loo–Riegelman for 2-compartment.
- Two-compartment: C = Ae^(−αt) + Be^(−βt); k21 = (Aβ + Bα)/(A + B); k10 = αβ/k21; k12 = α + β − k21 − k10; V1 = D/(A + B); Vss = V1(1 + k12/k21); Vβ = CL/β. Drug Y: k21 0.56, k10 0.714, k12 0.926 h⁻¹; V1 10, Vss 26.5, Vβ 35.7 L.
- NCA: MRT = AUMC/AUC; MAT = MRToral − MRTiv = 1/Ka; Vss = CL × MRT; tail AUC = Clast/λz.
- Drug X: K 0.1733 h⁻¹, t½ 4 h, Vd 25 L, CL 4.33 L/h, AUC(500 mg IV) 115.4, oral AUC 93.67 (trapezoid), F 0.81, MRT oral 6.55 h, MAT 0.78 h.

## Unit 4 — Nonlinear PK and interactions

- Signs: AUC/dose not constant, t½ changes with dose.
- Rate = Vmax C/(Km + C); Css = Km R/(Vmax − R); CL = Vmax/(Km + C).
- Two steady states: Km = (R2 − R1)/(R1/C1 − R2/C2); Vmax = R1 + Km R1/C1. Plot R vs R/Css: slope −Km, intercept Vmax.
- t90 = [Km Vd/(Vmax − R)²](2.3 Vmax − 0.9R). Drug Z: Vmax 500 mg/day, Km 4 mg/L → 300 → 6, 400 → 16 mg/L.
- Displacement: low-extraction → unbound level unchanged at steady state; high-extraction IV → unbound AUC ↑; oral AUCu = Dose/CLint.
- Tissue binding: Vd = Vp + VT fu/fuT.
- AUCR = 1/[fm/(1 + [I]/Ki) + (1 − fm)]; strong ≥ 5, moderate 2–5, weak 1.25–2. Induction (PXR/CAR) takes 1–2 weeks.
- ICH M12 transporters: P-gp, BCRP, OATP1B1/1B3, OAT1/3, OCT2, MATE1/2-K.

## Unit 5 — BA/BE, BCS, biosimilars

- F = (AUCoral DoseIV)/(AUCIV Doseoral).
- 2 × 2 crossover, washout ≥ 5 t½, sampling ≥ 3 t½, AUC0–t ≥ 80% AUC0–∞, fasting/fed.
- ln AUC, ln Cmax; 90% CI of GMR within 80.00–125.00% (TOST); NTI 90.00–111.11%; HVD (CV ≥ 30%) replicate design, scaled Cmax limits up to 69.84–143.19%.
- Example: GMR 95.36%, CI 88.81–102.40%, CVw 9.6% → BE.
- India: CDSCO, NDCT Rules 2019, ethics committee, CTRI, BA/BE guideline 2005.
- BCS (ICH M9): solubility in ≤ 250 mL over pH 1.2–6.8 at 37 °C; fa ≥ 85%; very rapid 85%/15 min, rapid 85%/30 min; waivers Class I and III.
- Biosimilar: stepwise comparability, analytical first, PK/PD, immunogenicity, extrapolation; India Similar Biologics guidelines 2012/2016.

## Unit 6 — Applications

- Emax: E = Emax C/(EC50 + C); sigmoid Cⁿ. Anticlockwise loop → ke0 effect compartment; clockwise → tolerance. Indirect response: kin/kout.
- ER design: k0r = Css CL/F; DL = Css Vd/F; Di = DL − k0r tmax. Drug X (Css 4 mg/L, 12 h): 21.7 mg/h, 260 mg, loading 84 mg.
- %PTF = (Cmax − Cmin)/Cav × 100; dose dumping; MR BE fasted + fed.
- Targeting: EPR, MPS, PEGylation; DTI = (T/NT carrier)/(T/NT free) (example 8).
- Proteins: lymphatic SC absorption, proteolysis, renal filtration < 60 kDa, TMDD; PEG/Fc/albumin extend t½.
- mAbs: FcRn recycling (t½ about 2–3 weeks), TMDD nonlinear, ADA.
- Oligonucleotides: short plasma, long tissue t½; GalNAc–ASGPR; nucleases.
- Vaccines: titre kinetics, adjuvants, prime–boost. Gene therapy: biodistribution, shedding, expression; CAR-T expansion.

questions.answer:
1. Statement: only the un-ionised, lipid-soluble form of a weak electrolyte crosses the GI membrane by passive diffusion; absorption depends on pKa, GI pH and lipophilicity (Brodie, Shore, Schanker).
2. Henderson–Hasselbalch: weak acid pH − pKa = log([A⁻]/[HA]) → % un-ionised = 100/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)); weak base pKa − pH = log([BH⁺]/[B]) → % un-ionised = 100/(1 + 10^(pKa − pH)).
3. Example: acid pKa 4.4 is 99.9% un-ionised at pH 1.2 but 0.4% at pH 6.8; base pKa 9.0 is 0.6% un-ionised at pH 6.8.
4. Ion trapping: at equilibrium total-drug ratio for an acid = (1 + 10^(pH2 − pKa))/(1 + 10^(pH1 − pKa)); acid pKa 3.5 between pH 1.4 and 7.4 gives about 7,900 : 1 in favour of plasma.
5. Limitation 1: small intestine absorbs most weak acids despite ionisation because of its huge surface and long residence.
6. Limitation 2: microclimate pH (about 5.5–6.5) next to the mucosa differs from bulk pH.
7. Limitation 3: unstirred water layer limits very lipophilic drugs.
8. Limitation 4: ionised species cross by paracellular route, ion pairs and carriers; efflux and gut-wall metabolism ignored.
9. Limitation 5: dissolution and solubility not considered; log P/log D also matters.
10. Uses: explains direction of pH effects, ion trapping, urinary pH effects on excretion, choice of salt forms.
questions.question: Discuss the pH-partition theory of drug absorption. Derive the expressions for the fraction un-ionised of weak acids and bases and explain the limitations of the theory with examples.

questions.answer:
1. Dissolution steps: wetting, detachment of molecules, diffusion through the stagnant layer to bulk.
2. Noyes–Whitney (Nernst–Brunner film theory): dM/dt = DA(Cs − C)/h; under sink conditions rate ≈ DACs/h. Define each symbol.
3. Interfacial barrier model: interfacial transport is slow; rate = Ki(Cs − C).
4. Danckwerts surface-renewal model: eddies renew the surface; rate = A(Cs − C)√(γD).
5. Hixson–Crowell cube-root law for shrinking particles: W0^(1/3) − W^(1/3) = κt.
6. Drug factors: solubility, particle size and surface area (micronisation; 5-fold smaller diameter gives 5-fold area), polymorphism, amorphous state, hydrates/solvates, salt form (diffusion-layer pH), wettability, complexation.
7. Formulation factors: diluents, disintegrants (superdisintegrants), binders, lubricants (magnesium stearate film), surfactants, coatings.
8. Processing factors: granulation method, compression force (porosity), drying, ageing on storage.
9. Test/medium factors: agitation (h), temperature, viscosity, pH, volume (sink).
10. Conclude: control of these factors is essential for BCS II drugs where dissolution limits absorption.
questions.question: Explain the Noyes–Whitney equation and other theories of drug dissolution. Discuss the physicochemical, formulation and processing factors affecting the dissolution rate.

questions.answer:
1. In vitro: PAMPA (artificial lipid membrane; passive only); Caco-2 monolayers (21-day culture, TEER check, Papp = (dQ/dt)/(A C0), bidirectional efflux ratio ≥ 2 suggests efflux); MDCK and MDCK-MDR1; Ussing chamber; everted sac.
2. In situ: single-pass intestinal perfusion in rat with water-flux marker, Peff = −Q ln(Cout/Cin)/(2πrL); closed-loop (Doluisio); intestinal–vascular perfusion.
3. In vivo: human jejunal perfusion (Loc-I-Gut, double-balloon 10 cm segment); mass balance and absolute bioavailability to find fa (≥ 85% = high permeability, ICH M9); deconvolution.
4. Advantages/limits: in vitro fast but laboratory-specific, validated with reference drugs; in situ keeps blood supply; in vivo most relevant but costly.
5. Transport model: flux J = Peff × C; 1/Peff = 1/PABL + 1/(Pm + Ppara).
6. Pm = P0 × fneutral: permeability falls ten-fold per pH unit of ionisation until a paracellular floor.
7. Unstirred layer limits highly lipophilic drugs; the apparent pKa shifts.
8. Maximum flux = Peff × Cs; ionisation raises solubility but lowers permeability (trade-off behind BCS).
9. GIT properties: mucus, bile micelles, microclimate pH 5.5–6.5, intracellular pH 7.0–7.2, tight junctions (claudins, occludin, ZO) favour small cations.
questions.question: Describe in vitro, in situ and in vivo methods to determine drug permeability. Add a note on the transport model (permeability–solubility–charge state).

questions.answer:
1. Rate order: solution > suspension > capsule > tablet > coated tablet.
2. Solution: no dissolution step; risks of precipitation on dilution (salts, cosolvents), viscosity slows emptying, complexation.
3. Suspension: fine wetted particles dissolve quickly; particle size, wetting agent, viscosity, crystal growth and polymorph matter.
4. Capsule: shell dissolves fast; powder plug must deaggregate; diluent, lubricant, packing density, gelatin cross-linking on ageing.
5. Tablet: disintegration → granules → particles (Wagner scheme); compression force, binder, disintegrant, lubricant, coating add delays.
questions.question: Explain the role of the dosage form (solution, suspension, capsule, tablet) in gastrointestinal absorption.

questions.answer:
1. Thin acidic layer (about pH 5.5–6.5) at the enterocyte surface, created by the apical Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger and held by mucus; bulk lumen pH is higher (6.5–7.5).
2. Weak acids: more un-ionised at the membrane than bulk pH predicts → better absorption than pH-partition calculation suggests.
3. Weak bases: more ionised at the surface → lower passive permeability.
4. Explains part of the failure of the classical pH-partition hypothesis.
5. Intracellular pH (7.0–7.2) and blood pH 7.4 then pull weak acids across (ionisation inside the cell).
questions.question: What is pH microclimate? How does it influence the absorption of weak acids and weak bases?

questions.answer:
1. Seal between adjacent epithelial cells at the apical side; proteins claudins, occludin, junctional adhesion molecules linked to actin via ZO-1/2/3.
2. Below it lie adherens junctions and desmosomes.

# Unit 1: Drug absorption from the gastrointestinal tract

This unit explains how an oral drug moves from the dosage form into the blood: the structure of the gut, the routes across the epithelium, the pH-partition hypothesis and its limits, dissolution theory, the effect of each dosage form, and the modern "transport model" that links permeability, solubility and charge state. It ends with the experimental methods used to measure solubility and permeability.

All numbers in worked examples are example numbers for hypothetical drugs, chosen to make the arithmetic clear.

## 1.1 The gastrointestinal tract as an absorbing organ

```text
 Dosage form
     │  disintegration / deaggregation
     ▼
 Drug particles in GI fluid ──dissolution──► Drug in solution
                                                 │  permeation across epithelium
                                                 ▼
                                       Portal blood → liver (first pass) → systemic blood
```

| Region | Typical pH (fasted) | Transit | Main features |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stomach | 1–3 (rises to 3–5 after a meal) | 0.5–2 h, depends on meal | Small surface, mixing and grinding; little absorption of most drugs |
| Duodenum | about 5–6.5 | minutes | Bile and pancreatic juice enter; rapid pH rise |
| Jejunum | about 6–7 | together with ileum about 3–4 h | Largest absorbing surface (folds, villi, microvilli), many transporters |
| Ileum | about 7–7.5 | | Bile salt reabsorption, Peyer's patches (M-cells) |
| Colon | about 5.5–7 | 10–30 h or more | Long residence, bacteria, less fluid; site for colon-targeted and some extended-release absorption |

**Why the small intestine absorbs most drugs:** the folds of Kerckring, villi and microvilli multiply the surface greatly; blood flow is high; residence time is several hours; and the epithelium carries many uptake transporters. The stomach mainly decides *when* the drug reaches the intestine.

**Gastric emptying.** In the fasted state the stomach follows the migrating motor complex (MMC), a cycle of about 1.5–2 h: phase I (quiet), phase II (irregular contractions) and phase III (strong "housekeeper" waves that sweep undissolved material, including non-disintegrating tablets, into the intestine). A meal stops the MMC and the stomach empties slowly in the fed pattern. Fat, high calorie load, acidity, cold or very hot liquids and some drugs (anticholinergics, opioids) slow emptying; metoclopramide speeds it. Because most drugs are absorbed in the intestine, slower emptying usually delays tmax and may lower Cmax.

**Other physiological factors:** intestinal transit time, blood flow to the gut, luminal enzymes (peptidases degrade peptides), gut-wall metabolism (CYP3A4 in enterocytes), efflux transporters (P-glycoprotein, BCRP), disease (achlorhydria, malabsorption, Crohn's disease), age, and food (bile release improves solubility of lipophilic drugs; binding to food can reduce absorption).

## 1.2 Mechanisms of drug absorption

| Mechanism | Driving force / carrier | Saturable? | Typical substrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Passive transcellular diffusion | Concentration gradient of the un-ionised, lipid-soluble form (Fick's law) | No | Most small lipophilic drugs |
| Paracellular diffusion | Through tight junctions between cells | No | Small hydrophilic molecules, some cations |
| Carrier-mediated: facilitated diffusion | Carrier, no energy, down the gradient | Yes | Some sugars, vitamins |
| Carrier-mediated: active transport | Carrier, energy (ATP or ion gradient), can work against a gradient | Yes, shows competition | Amino acid and peptide-like drugs (PEPT1 substrates such as β-lactams and ACE-inhibitor prodrugs), nucleosides |
| Efflux (active, secretory direction) | ABC transporters P-gp, BCRP, MRP2 pump drug back into the lumen | Yes | Many lipophilic drugs; lowers net absorption |
| Endocytosis (pinocytosis, receptor-mediated, phagocytosis) | Membrane vesicles | Yes | Macromolecules, particles, vitamin B12–intrinsic factor complex |
| Ion-pair transport | A charged drug pairs with an endogenous counter-ion and the neutral pair diffuses | — | Quaternary ammonium compounds |
| Lymphatic uptake (M-cells, chylomicrons) | Via lipoproteins and lymph | — | Very lipophilic drugs (log P above about 5) given with fat, particulates |

**Fick's first law for passive diffusion**

dQ/dt = (D × K × A / h) × (CGI − Cplasma) = P × A × ΔC

where D is the diffusion coefficient in the membrane, K the membrane/water partition coefficient, A the area, h the membrane thickness and P (= DK/h) the permeability coefficient. Because blood flow removes absorbed drug rapidly, Cplasma is much smaller than CGI ("sink condition") and absorption follows apparent first-order kinetics: rate = Ka × amount at the absorption site.

**Carrier-mediated transport** follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics: rate = Jmax × C/(Kt + C). At low concentration it is near first order; at high concentration it saturates and becomes zero order, so the fraction of a large dose absorbed falls. It is structure-specific and can be inhibited competitively.

## 1.3 pH-partition theory of drug absorption

**Statement (Brodie, Shore and Schanker):** in the GI tract, only the un-ionised form of a weak acid or weak base, if it is lipid-soluble enough, crosses the membrane by passive diffusion. The fraction un-ionised depends on the pKa of the drug and the pH at the absorption site (Henderson–Hasselbalch):

- Weak acid: % un-ionised = 100 / (1 + 10^(pH − pKa))
- Weak base: % un-ionised = 100 / (1 + 10^(pKa − pH))

At steady state, if only the un-ionised form crosses and its concentration is equal on both sides, the ratio of total drug concentrations across a membrane separating two pH values is:

- Weak acid: Rplasma/GI = [1 + 10^(pHplasma − pKa)] / [1 + 10^(pHGI − pKa)]
- Weak base: RGI/plasma = [1 + 10^(pKa − pHGI)] / [1 + 10^(pKa − pHplasma)]

### Worked example 1 (example numbers)

A weak acid of pKa 4.4 is un-ionised to 99.94% at pH 1.2, 0.40% at pH 6.8 and 0.10% at pH 7.4. A weak base of pKa 9.0 is un-ionised to 0.63% at pH 6.8 and 2.45% at pH 7.4, and is almost completely ionised at pH 1.2.

For a weak acid of pKa 3.5 with gastric pH 1.4 and plasma pH 7.4:

R = (1 + 10^3.9)/(1 + 10^−2.1) = 7944/1.008 ≈ **7,880**

so total drug at equilibrium would be about 7,900 times higher in plasma than in the stomach: the acid is "trapped" in plasma (ion trapping). For a weak base of pKa 8.5 the ratio stomach/plasma is about 9 × 10^5, which is why weak bases given intravenously can accumulate in gastric juice.

### Limitations of the pH-partition hypothesis

1. **Surface area and residence time dominate.** Weak acids are absorbed mainly in the small intestine, where they are highly ionised, because its surface is huge and contact time long. The stomach's favourable pH cannot outweigh its small area.
2. **Microclimate pH.** The layer next to the enterocyte surface is more acidic (about 5.5–6) than the bulk intestinal fluid, which increases the un-ionised fraction of weak acids at the membrane.
3. **Ionised forms do cross.** Paracellular diffusion, ion-pairs and transporters carry charged species; the ionised form has a small but real permeability.
4. **Unstirred (aqueous boundary) layer.** For very lipophilic drugs, diffusion through the water layer next to the membrane, not membrane partitioning, limits the rate.
5. **Ignores dissolution.** A poorly soluble drug may never reach a high enough solution concentration.
6. **Ignores carriers and efflux, gut-wall metabolism, and binding to mucus.**
7. **Lipid solubility (log P or log D) also matters,** not only the un-ionised fraction; a fully un-ionised but very polar molecule is still poorly absorbed.

Despite these, the hypothesis correctly predicts the *direction* of pH effects and explains ion trapping, urinary pH effects on excretion, and the use of buffered or salt forms.

## 1.4 Formulation and physicochemical factors: dissolution

For most solid oral products, **dissolution is the rate-limiting step for poorly soluble drugs**, and **permeation is rate-limiting for soluble but poorly permeable drugs**.

### Dissolution process and models

```text
 Solid surface │ stagnant diffusion layer (thickness h) │ bulk solution
   C = Cs      │ ───────── concentration falls ──────►  │  C (bulk)
```

**Noyes–Whitney equation** (with the Nernst–Brunner film interpretation):

dM/dt = D × A × (Cs − C) / h

- dM/dt: dissolution rate (mass per time)
- D: diffusion coefficient of the drug in the medium
- A: surface area of the dissolving solid
- Cs: saturation solubility at the surface; C: bulk concentration
- h: thickness of the diffusion (stagnant) layer

When C is much smaller than Cs (sink conditions, in practice C below about 10–30% of Cs), rate ≈ D A Cs / h, i.e. constant.

**Other models**

- **Interfacial barrier model:** the slow step is the reaction or detachment at the solid–liquid interface, not diffusion; rate = Ki (Cs − C).
- **Danckwerts surface-renewal model:** turbulent eddies continually replace fluid at the surface; rate = A (Cs − C) √(γD), where γ is the rate of surface renewal.
- **Hixson–Crowell cube-root law** for a powder of equal spheres dissolving with shrinking area: W0^(1/3) − W^(1/3) = κ t.

### Worked example 2 — Noyes–Whitney (example numbers)

D = 5 × 10⁻⁶ cm²/s, A = 50 cm², h = 30 µm (3 × 10⁻³ cm), Cs = 1.0 mg/mL, C = 0.05 mg/mL.

dM/dt = 5 × 10⁻⁶ × 50 × (1.0 − 0.05)/(3 × 10⁻³) = 0.0792 mg/s = **4.75 mg/min**.

Particle size effect: 100 mg of powder (density 1.3 g/cm³) as spheres of diameter d has surface S = 6m/(ρd). At d = 50 µm, S = 92 cm²; at d = 10 µm, S = 462 cm². A five-fold smaller diameter gives a five-fold larger area and, other terms constant, a five-fold faster initial dissolution.

### Worked example 3 — Hixson–Crowell (example numbers)

A powder sample of 100 mg leaves 64 mg undissolved after 10 min. κ = (100^(1/3) − 64^(1/3))/10 = (4.642 − 4.000)/10 = 0.0642 mg^(1/3)/min. Time for complete dissolution = 100^(1/3)/κ ≈ **72 min**.

### Factors affecting the dissolution rate

| Group | Factor | Effect and explanation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drug (physicochemical) | Solubility (Cs) | Directly proportional in Noyes–Whitney |
| | Particle size / surface area | Micronisation and nanosizing increase A; very fine hydrophobic powders may aggregate or float, so effective area matters |
| | Polymorphism | Metastable polymorphs have higher free energy and higher solubility; may convert to the stable form on storage |
| | Amorphous state | Higher solubility than crystalline; basis of solid dispersions; risk of recrystallisation |
| | Hydrates and solvates | Anhydrous forms usually dissolve faster than hydrates in water; organic solvates may dissolve faster |
| | Salt form | Salts of weak acids or bases dissolve faster; a sodium salt of a weak acid raises the pH of the diffusion layer, increasing local solubility |
| | Wettability | Contact angle; surfactants improve wetting |
| | Complexation, prodrugs, cocrystals | Change apparent solubility |
| Formulation | Diluents | Hydrophilic diluents (lactose) help wetting; adsorbents can bind drug |
| | Disintegrants | Superdisintegrants (croscarmellose, crospovidone, sodium starch glycolate) increase area quickly |
| | Binders | Excess binder or strong binders slow disintegration |
| | Lubricants | Hydrophobic magnesium stearate coats particles and slows dissolution, worse with long mixing |
| | Surfactants | Improve wetting and solubilise (micelles) |
| | Coatings | Film coats add a lag; enteric coats delay release until intestinal pH |
| Processing | Granulation method | Wet granulation often improves wetting; dry granulation may slow it |
| | Compression force | Higher force lowers porosity and slows disintegration; very high force can fracture particles and increase area |
| | Storage | Ageing, moisture uptake and hardening can slow dissolution |
| Medium / test | Agitation | Faster agitation reduces h |
| | Temperature, viscosity, pH, volume, surface tension | Affect Cs, D and h |

## 1.5 Gastrointestinal absorption: the role of the dosage form

General order of rate of drug availability (fastest to slowest): **solution > suspension > capsule > tablet > coated tablet** (modified-release products are designed to be slow).

### Solutions (elixirs, syrups, solutions)

- No dissolution step, so absorption is usually fastest and most complete.
- Factors: dilution in gastric fluid may **precipitate** a weak acid from its salt solution (fine precipitate usually redissolves quickly); viscosity of syrups slows gastric emptying and diffusion; cosolvents (ethanol, propylene glycol) may precipitate drug on dilution; complexation (with cyclodextrins or other ingredients) can reduce free drug; chemical stability in solution limits use.

### Suspensions

- Dissolution of fine, already wetted particles is rapid.
- Key factors: particle size and size distribution, polymorphic form, wetting agent, viscosity (high viscosity slows dissolution and emptying), crystal growth on storage (Ostwald ripening), drug–excipient complexation and the density of the vehicle.

### Capsules (hard gelatin)

- The shell dissolves quickly in warm acidic fluid; then the powder plug must deaggregate.
- Factors: particle size, hydrophilic versus hydrophobic diluent, lubricant, wetting agent, tightness of packing (dense plugs dissolve slowly), and shell cross-linking on ageing (aldehydes or high humidity make gelatin less soluble; pepsin or pancreatin may be added to the test medium in such cases).
- Soft gelatin capsules with drug dissolved in oil or a self-emulsifying system can give fast, reproducible absorption of lipophilic drugs.

### Tablets

- Must disintegrate into granules and then fine particles before most dissolution occurs. Granules dissolve faster than the intact tablet, and primary particles faster still (Wagner's scheme).

```text
 Tablet ──disintegration──► Granules ──deaggregation──► Fine particles
    │ (slow)                    │ (moderate)                │ (fast)
    └──────────────────── drug in solution ◄──────────────┘
                                │ absorption
                                ▼
                        drug in blood
```

- Factors: compression force, binder and disintegrant type and amount, lubricant, granule size, porosity, coating. Sugar coating and film coating add time; enteric coating moves release to the intestine; changes in coating thickness change lag time.

### Dissolution methods (summary)

Official methods (IP, USP, BP): basket (Apparatus 1), paddle (Apparatus 2), reciprocating cylinder (3), flow-through cell (4), paddle over disc (5), rotating cylinder (6) and reciprocating holder (7). Details, alternatives and acceptance criteria are covered in Unit 2.

### Formulation and processing factors

Choice of salt or polymorph, particle size, excipient compatibility, granulation route, compression and coating determine product performance; they are deliberately controlled in quality by design (Unit 2).

### Correlation of in vivo data with in vitro dissolution data

The aim is a predictive mathematical link between an in vitro property (usually rate or extent of dissolution) and an in vivo response (plasma level, AUC, Cmax or fraction absorbed). Level A (point-to-point), B (mean dissolution time vs mean residence time) and C (single point) correlations, and their regulatory uses (biowaivers, setting dissolution specifications), are described in Unit 2. A correlation is most likely when dissolution is the rate-limiting step (BCS Class II).

## 1.6 The transport model: permeability, solubility and charge state

Modern biopharmaceutics (for example the treatment by Avdeef) combines the pH-partition hypothesis with diffusion through barriers in series.

### Flux and the effective permeability

Flux across the intestinal wall: J = Peff × C (C = dissolved drug concentration at the surface). Drug must cross several resistances in series, like electrical resistors:

1/Peff = 1/PABL + 1/(Pm + Ppara)

- **PABL:** permeability of the aqueous boundary (unstirred) layer; depends on the diffusion coefficient and layer thickness, not on lipophilicity.
- **Pm:** membrane (transcellular) permeability; for a weak acid or base only the neutral species crosses well, so Pm = P0 × fneutral, where P0 is the intrinsic permeability of the neutral form.
- **Ppara:** paracellular permeability through tight junctions.

Consequences:

- At pH values where the drug is mostly neutral, Pm is large and **PABL limits** the flux (log Peff vs pH curve flattens).
- Where the drug is mostly ionised, Pm falls by a factor of 10 for each pH unit away from the pKa until Ppara or the small permeability of the ion sets a floor.
- The apparent pKa seen in permeability–pH curves shifts from the true pKa because of the boundary layer ("pKa flux").

### Solubility × permeability = flux

The maximum flux depends on *both*: Jmax = Peff × Cs. A highly soluble but impermeable drug and a highly permeable but insoluble drug can both have low flux. Charge state works in opposite directions: ionisation raises solubility but lowers membrane permeability. This trade-off underlies the BCS (Unit 5). A simple estimate is the **maximum absorbable dose**:

MAD = S × Ka × SIWV × SITT

(S solubility at pH 6.5, Ka transintestinal absorption rate constant, SIWV small-intestinal water volume about 250 mL, SITT small-intestinal transit time about 270 min.)

**Example (example numbers):** S = 0.05 mg/mL, Ka = 0.03 min⁻¹ → MAD = 0.05 × 0.03 × 250 × 270 = **about 101 mg**. A planned 200 mg dose would be solubility-limited; the dose number D0 = (200/250)/0.05 = 16 (well above 1).

### Properties of the GIT relevant to the model

- **Surface area and villus structure** set the available area.
- **Mucus layer** (glycoproteins) and the unstirred water layer slow diffusion of lipophilic and large molecules; mucus binds some cationic drugs.
- **Bile salts and lipids** form mixed micelles that raise the apparent solubility of lipophilic drugs (food effect, FaSSIF and FeSSIF media).
- **Transit and fluid volume:** fluid is not uniformly spread; pockets of fluid and short residence limit dissolution.

### pH microclimate

The Na⁺/H⁺ exchanger on the apical membrane pumps protons into a thin layer near the surface that is held by mucus. Its pH is about 5.5–6.5 while the bulk lumen may be 6.5–7.5. For weak acids this raises the neutral fraction at the membrane; for weak bases it lowers it. It explains why weak acids are absorbed better from the jejunum than bulk-pH calculations predict.

### Intracellular pH environment

The cytoplasm of enterocytes is about pH 7.0–7.2, and blood is 7.4. A weak acid entering the cell becomes more ionised and is "pulled" through towards the blood side; a weak base may be partly trapped in acidic intracellular compartments (lysosomes, pH about 4.5–5), which increases its tissue retention. The pH gradient across the cell therefore adds a driving force beyond simple concentration.

### Tight-junction complex

```text
  Lumen
  ┌─────────┐ tight junction ┌─────────┐
  │ cell    │╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳╳│ cell    │   ← claudins, occludin, ZO proteins
  │         │ adherens jn    │         │
  │         │  desmosome     │         │
  └─────────┘                └─────────┘
  Blood / lamina propria
```

- Seals adjacent enterocytes; formed by transmembrane proteins (claudins, occludin, junctional adhesion molecules) linked to the actin cytoskeleton through zonula occludens (ZO) proteins.
- The paracellular route is narrow (pores of a few ångströms) and leakier in the upper small intestine than in the colon.
- It favours small hydrophilic molecules (molecular weight below about 200–300 Da) and, because the pores carry negative charges, **cations pass more easily than anions**.
- Paracellular area is only a tiny fraction of the total surface, so this route is minor for most drugs.
- **Permeation enhancers** (medium-chain fatty acids such as sodium caprate, chitosan, bile salts, EDTA) open tight junctions transiently; they are used in some oral peptide products.

## 1.7 Solubility: experimental methods

| Method | What it measures | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shake-flask (equilibrium or thermodynamic) | Concentration of a saturated solution in equilibrium with excess solid at fixed temperature (37 °C for biopharmaceutics) | Gold standard; shake 24–72 h, separate by filtration or centrifugation, assay by HPLC or UV; check pH at the end and the solid form (polymorph or salt conversion) |
| pH–solubility profile | Shake-flask at several pH values across 1.2–6.8 | Needed for BCS solubility class; gives intrinsic solubility S0 and pKa-related curve |
| Kinetic solubility | Concentration at which drug added from a DMSO stock precipitates, detected by nephelometry, turbidity or UV | High-throughput screening in discovery; often overestimates (supersaturation, amorphous precipitate) |
| Potentiometric (acid–base titration, e.g. "CheqSol") | Intrinsic solubility of ionisable drugs from titration curves | Small sample, fast |
| Biorelevant media | Solubility in FaSSIF, FeSSIF, FaSSGF | Shows food and bile effects for lipophilic drugs |
| Phase-solubility (Higuchi–Connors) | Solubility vs complexing-agent concentration | Studies cyclodextrin complexes |

## 1.8 Permeability: in vitro, in situ and in vivo methods

### In vitro

1. **PAMPA (parallel artificial membrane permeability assay):** a filter coated with lipid in an organic solvent separates donor and acceptor wells; measures passive transcellular permeability only. Fast and cheap; no transporters, no paracellular route.
2. **Caco-2 monolayers:** human colon carcinoma cells grown on filters for about 21 days differentiate into enterocyte-like cells with tight junctions, brush border and transporters (P-gp, BCRP, PEPT1). Integrity is checked by trans-epithelial electrical resistance (TEER) and markers (lucifer yellow, mannitol). Apparent permeability:

   Papp = (dQ/dt) / (A × C0)

   Bidirectional studies (apical→basolateral and basolateral→apical) give the **efflux ratio** = Papp(B→A)/Papp(A→B); a ratio of about 2 or more suggests active efflux, confirmed with an inhibitor.
3. **MDCK and MDCK-MDR1 cells:** grow faster (3–5 days), lower background transporter expression; MDR1-transfected cells test P-gp efflux.
4. **Excised tissue:** Ussing chamber (mounted intestinal segment, measures flux and electrical parameters), everted gut sac (drug transfer into the sac), intestinal rings for uptake.

**Example (example numbers):** a Caco-2 insert of area 1.12 cm², donor concentration 100 µg/mL, steady appearance in the receiver 0.12 µg/min.
Papp = (0.12/60 µg/s)/(1.12 cm² × 100 µg/cm³) = **1.8 × 10⁻⁵ cm/s**, which is in the high-permeability range for most laboratories (each laboratory classifies against its own reference drugs).

### In situ

- **Single-pass intestinal perfusion (SPIP) in rats:** a segment of jejunum is cannulated and perfused at a fixed flow Q with drug solution; inlet and outlet concentrations (corrected for water flux with a non-absorbed marker) give

  Peff = −Q × ln(Cout/Cin) / (2πrL)

  where r is the radius and L the length of the segment. Blood supply and innervation are intact.
- **Closed-loop (Doluisio) method:** a tied segment filled with drug solution; samples taken from the loop over time.
- **Intestinal–vascular perfusion:** drug appearance in mesenteric blood is measured directly.

### In vivo

- **Human regional jejunal perfusion (Loc-I-Gut):** a multichannel tube with two balloons isolates a 10 cm segment of jejunum; Peff in humans is measured directly. Human Peff values classify BCS permeability.
- **Mass-balance and absolute bioavailability studies:** fraction absorbed (fa) from urinary recovery of total radioactivity after oral and IV doses, or from absolute bioavailability corrected for first-pass loss. Under ICH M9, fa of 85% or more means high permeability.
- **Pharmacokinetic deconvolution** (Wagner–Nelson, Loo–Riegelman; Unit 3) gives the time course of absorption.

## 1.9 Linking the pieces

```text
 Dose ─► Disintegration ─► Dissolution (Noyes–Whitney: D, A, Cs, h)
                                │
                                ▼
            Dissolved drug at gut surface (pH microclimate, charge state)
                                │  Peff = f(ABL, membrane P0·fneutral, paracellular)
                                ▼
          Enterocyte (CYP3A4, P-gp efflux, pH 7.0–7.2) ─► portal blood ─► liver ─► F
```

Oral bioavailability: **F = fa × FG × FH**, where fa is the fraction absorbed into the gut wall, FG the fraction escaping gut-wall metabolism and FH the fraction escaping hepatic first pass. Biopharmaceutic design works mainly on fa (solubility, dissolution, permeability).

## Remember

- Rate-limiting step: dissolution for poorly soluble drugs, permeation for poorly permeable ones.
- pH-partition: only the un-ionised, lipid-soluble form diffuses; % un-ionised acid = 100/(1 + 10^(pH − pKa)), base = 100/(1 + 10^(pKa − pH)).
- Limits of pH-partition: intestinal surface area, microclimate pH, unstirred layer, carriers and ion pairs, dissolution.
- Noyes–Whitney: dM/dt = DA(Cs − C)/h; sink condition keeps C small; Hixson–Crowell is the cube-root law.
- Dosage form order: solution > suspension > capsule > tablet > coated tablet.
- Transport model: 1/Peff = 1/PABL + 1/(Pm + Ppara); Pm = P0 × fneutral; flux = Peff × Cs.
- Microclimate pH about 5.5–6.5; intracellular pH about 7.0–7.2; tight junctions favour small hydrophilic cations.
- Permeability methods: PAMPA, Caco-2 (efflux ratio ≥ 2), MDCK, Ussing chamber; SPIP Peff = −Q ln(Cout/Cin)/(2πrL); Loc-I-Gut; fa ≥ 85% = high permeability.
- F = fa × FG × FH.

# Unit 2: Biopharmaceutic considerations in drug product design and in vitro drug product performance

This unit asks a practical question: how do we design an oral product so that the drug reaches the blood at the right rate and extent, and how do we prove it in the laboratory? It covers the biopharmaceutic factors that decide bioavailability, rate-limiting steps, the physicochemical nature of the drug, formulation factors, compendial and alternative dissolution tests, meeting dissolution specifications, sources of variability, in vitro–in vivo correlation (IVIVC), comparison of dissolution profiles, stability and the overall design of a drug product.

All numbers in worked examples are example numbers for hypothetical products.

## 2.1 Introduction

A **drug product** is the drug plus excipients in a dosage form made by a defined process. Two products with the same amount of the same drug can give very different plasma levels because of differences in particle size, salt, polymorph, excipients or process. **Biopharmaceutics** studies how these physicochemical and formulation variables affect the rate and extent of absorption. Its goals in product design are:

- adequate and reproducible bioavailability;
- the intended release profile (immediate, delayed, extended);
- a quality-control test (usually dissolution) that is discriminating and, ideally, predictive of in vivo behaviour;
- stability of that performance over the shelf life.

## 2.2 Biopharmaceutic factors affecting drug bioavailability

| Group | Factors |
| --- | --- |
| Drug substance | Solubility and pH–solubility profile, pKa, lipophilicity (log P, log D), particle size and surface area, crystal form (polymorphs, amorphous, solvates), salt form, chemical stability in GI fluids, complexation, molecular size |
| Drug product | Type of dosage form, excipients (diluents, binders, disintegrants, lubricants, surfactants, coating polymers), manufacturing process (granulation, compression force, drying), release mechanism |
| Patient (physiology) | GI pH, gastric emptying and transit, food, bile, fluid volume, gut-wall enzymes and transporters, first-pass metabolism, disease, age, concomitant drugs |
| Route | Oral, buccal, rectal, IM, SC, transdermal: each has its own barriers and blood flow |

## 2.3 Rate-limiting steps in drug absorption

For a solid oral product the steps are in series:

```text
 Solid dosage form ─k_dis─► particles ─k_d (dissolution)─► drug in solution ─Ka (permeation)─► blood
```

The **slowest step controls the overall rate**.

- **Dissolution rate-limited** (kd much smaller than Ka): typical for poorly soluble drugs (BCS II). Anything that speeds dissolution (micronisation, salt, solid dispersion, surfactant) speeds absorption; dissolution testing is likely to correlate with in vivo data.
- **Permeation rate-limited** (Ka much smaller than kd): typical for soluble but poorly permeable drugs (BCS III). Formulation changes in dissolution have little effect; permeation enhancers or prodrugs are needed.
- **Disintegration-limited:** for hard tablets or old capsules.
- **Gastric emptying-limited:** for rapidly dissolving, well-absorbed drugs, the rate of arrival in the intestine sets tmax.
- **For extended-release products,** release from the product is deliberately made the slowest step, so the plasma profile follows the release rate.

## 2.4 Physicochemical nature of the drug

1. **Solubility and dose.** The dose number D0 = (dose/250 mL)/Cs. If D0 is above 1, the dose cannot dissolve in a glass of water; absorption may be solubility-limited.
2. **pKa and pH–solubility profile.** Weak acids dissolve better in intestinal fluid; weak bases dissolve in the stomach but may precipitate when they enter the intestine (supersaturation and precipitation kinetics matter).
3. **Lipophilicity.** Log P of about 1–3 favours passive permeation; very high log P lowers aqueous solubility and increases binding.
4. **Particle size.** Smaller particles dissolve faster (larger area) and slightly more (Ostwald–Freundlich equation for very small particles). Nanocrystals and micronised powders are used for poorly soluble drugs.
5. **Polymorphism and amorphous forms.** Metastable forms and amorphous solids have higher apparent solubility; the risk is conversion to the stable, less soluble form during processing or storage. Regulatory filings must identify and control the form.
6. **Salt formation.** Common way to improve dissolution of ionisable drugs; the counter-ion also affects hygroscopicity, stability and manufacturability. A salt of a weak acid dissolves faster partly because it raises the pH of the diffusion layer.
7. **Hydrates, solvates and cocrystals.** Change solubility and stability.
8. **Chemical stability in GI fluids.** Acid-labile drugs need enteric coating or a stable prodrug.
9. **Complexation.** Cyclodextrins increase apparent solubility; complexes with insoluble excipients reduce availability.

## 2.5 Formulation factors affecting drug product performance

| Factor | Typical effect |
| --- | --- |
| Diluent | Hydrophilic diluents aid wetting; calcium salts can form insoluble complexes with some drugs (tetracyclines) |
| Binder | Concentration and type affect hardness and disintegration time |
| Disintegrant | Amount and position (intra- vs extra-granular) control break-up; superdisintegrants act at low levels |
| Lubricant | Hydrophobic magnesium stearate forms a film; over-mixing slows dissolution; hydrophilic lubricants are alternatives |
| Surfactant | Improves wetting and solubilisation; may also affect membrane permeability |
| Polymer (release-controlling) | Matrix (HPMC, ethylcellulose) or membrane coat controls release rate; viscosity grade and amount critical |
| Solubility enhancers | Solid dispersions, lipid-based systems (SEDDS), cyclodextrins, nanosuspensions |
| Process | Granulation, drying temperature, compression force, coating thickness and curing |

Excipient interactions can also change permeability (for example some surfactants inhibit P-gp) or stability.

## 2.6 In vitro dissolution and drug release testing

**Purpose:** quality control (batch-to-batch consistency), guide formulation development, detect process or stability changes, support biowaivers and, where an IVIVC exists, predict in vivo performance.

**Terms**

- **Dissolution test:** for immediate-release products.
- **Drug release test:** for modified-release products (delayed and extended release), usually multi-point.
- **Intrinsic dissolution rate (IDR):** dissolution rate per unit area of a pure drug compact with constant area (rotating disc, Wood's apparatus), in mg/min/cm². As a rough guide, an IDR above about 1 mg/min/cm² rarely gives dissolution-limited absorption, while one below about 0.1 mg/min/cm² usually does.

### Compendial methods of dissolution

| USP apparatus | Description | Typical use and conditions |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 Basket | Rotating mesh basket holding the unit | Capsules, floating products; often 50–100 rpm |
| 2 Paddle | Paddle stirrer in a round-bottom vessel; sinker for floating units | Most tablets; often 50–75 rpm |
| 3 Reciprocating cylinder | Glass cylinders move up and down through rows of media | Extended-release products; easy pH changes along the "GI tract" |
| 4 Flow-through cell | Fresh medium pumped through a cell holding the unit | Poorly soluble drugs (maintains sink), implants, powders, microspheres |
| 5 Paddle over disc | Paddle with the patch held on a disc | Transdermal patches |
| 6 Rotating cylinder | Patch fixed on a cylinder | Transdermal patches |
| 7 Reciprocating holder | Small units on a holder moving up and down | Small transdermal systems, implants, osmotic products |

The Indian Pharmacopoeia describes the basket (Apparatus I) and paddle (Apparatus II) and other apparatus for special products.

**Standard conditions (immediate-release, typical):** 900 mL medium (500–1000 mL), 37 ± 0.5 °C, deaerated medium, media of pH 1.2 (0.1 M HCl), 4.5 (acetate) and 6.8 (phosphate). Surfactants (for example sodium lauryl sulphate) may be added for poorly soluble drugs with justification. Sampling at fixed times, filtered immediately, assayed by UV or HPLC.

**Sink conditions:** the medium volume should be at least about three times the volume needed to saturate the dose, so that dissolution is not slowed by build-up of drug.

**Example (example numbers):** a 50 mg dose with Cs = 0.02 mg/mL needs 2,500 mL to dissolve; 900 mL would reach 2.8 × Cs, so sink is not possible (some drug cannot dissolve at all). With 0.5% surfactant raising Cs to 0.2 mg/mL, complete dissolution in 900 mL gives only 0.28 × Cs: sink conditions are met.

### Alternative methods of dissolution testing

- **Rotating-disc (intrinsic dissolution) and static-disc methods** for drug substance characterisation.
- **Beaker method (Levy) and flask–stirrer methods:** early simple designs.
- **Rotating bottle method:** for extended-release beads; bottles tumble end over end in a water bath.
- **Dialysis-bag and reverse-dialysis methods:** separate released drug from nanoparticles, liposomes and emulsions.
- **Biphasic dissolution:** an aqueous layer under an organic layer (octanol) that removes dissolved drug, mimicking absorption; useful for poorly soluble drugs.
- **Transfer models:** drug dissolved in simulated gastric fluid is pumped into simulated intestinal fluid to study precipitation of weak bases.
- **Biorelevant media:** FaSSGF, FaSSIF and FeSSIF contain bile salt and lecithin; they predict food effects better.
- **Dynamic GI models:** multi-compartment systems (for example the TNO gastro-intestinal model) mimic peristalsis, emptying, secretions and absorption.
- **Combined dissolution–permeation systems:** dissolution vessel linked to Caco-2 or artificial membranes.
- **Stress-test devices:** mimic mechanical forces of gastric emptying for extended-release products (dose dumping).

### Meeting dissolution requirements (USP-type acceptance tables)

**Immediate-release (Q = amount dissolved, as % of label claim, at the specified time):**

| Stage | Units tested | Acceptance criteria |
| --- | --- | --- |
| S1 | 6 | Each unit not less than Q + 5% |
| S2 | 6 more (12 total) | Average of 12 ≥ Q, and no unit below Q − 15% |
| S3 | 12 more (24 total) | Average of 24 ≥ Q, not more than 2 units below Q − 15%, and no unit below Q − 25% |

**Extended-release** uses levels L1 (6 units), L2 (12) and L3 (24) with limits at several time points (a range at each time and a minimum at the last point). **Delayed-release (enteric)** products are tested in an acid stage (A1–A3, limited release in 0.1 M HCl) followed by a buffer stage (B1–B3, Q in pH 6.8 buffer).

### Problems of variable control in dissolution testing

| Source | Examples | Control |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Apparatus | Vessel shape and finish, shaft wobble and centring, paddle or basket height, basket mesh damage, vibration from the bench or water bath | Mechanical calibration (dimensions, speed, wobble, centring, temperature) and performance verification with reference tablets |
| Medium | Wrong pH or ionic strength, dissolved gases forming bubbles on the unit, surfactant quality, evaporation | Prepare and check pH, deaerate, cover vessels |
| Hydrodynamics | "Coning" (a mound of undissolved powder under the paddle in Apparatus 2), unit sticking to the vessel, floating | Change speed with justification, use sinkers, consider Apparatus 1 |
| Sampling and analysis | Sampling position, filter adsorption or leaching, delayed filtration (continued dissolution), drug degradation in medium | Validated sampling zone, filter compatibility study, stability of samples |
| Product | Capsule cross-linking, hardening on storage | Enzymes (pepsin, pancreatin) in the medium for cross-linked gelatin; stability monitoring |
| Human | Timing errors, wrong calculations | Automation, training, second-person checks |

A **discriminating** method detects meaningful formulation or process changes; it should not be so harsh that every product passes or so mild that good batches fail.

## 2.7 Kinetics of drug release (models used to describe profiles)

| Model | Equation | Typical system |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zero order | Q = Q0 + k0 t | Osmotic pumps, reservoir systems, ideal extended release |
| First order | ln(100 − Q) = ln 100 − k1 t | Many immediate-release and porous matrix products |
| Higuchi | Q = kH √t | Drug diffusing from an insoluble matrix |
| Hixson–Crowell | W0^(1/3) − W^(1/3) = κ t | Erosion or dissolution with shrinking area |
| Korsmeyer–Peppas | Mt/M∞ = k tⁿ (first 60% of release) | Polymeric systems; n tells the mechanism |
| Weibull | M = 1 − exp[−(t − Ti)^b / a] | Empirical fit for many profiles |

For a thin film (slab), Korsmeyer–Peppas n = 0.5 means Fickian diffusion, 0.5 < n < 1 anomalous (diffusion plus swelling or erosion), and n = 1 Case II (zero-order, relaxation-controlled) transport. The limits are lower for cylinders (0.45 and 0.89) and spheres (0.43 and 0.85).

## 2.8 Performance of drug products: in vitro–in vivo correlation (IVIVC)

**Definition (US FDA, 1997 guidance on extended-release oral dosage forms):** a predictive mathematical model describing the relationship between an in vitro property of a dosage form (usually rate or extent of dissolution) and a relevant in vivo response (plasma concentration or amount absorbed).

| Level | What is correlated | Strength and use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Point-to-point: fraction dissolved in vitro vs fraction absorbed in vivo at each time (often 1:1 line) | Highest; whole plasma profile can be predicted; supports biowaivers for many changes and dissolution specifications |
| B | Mean in vitro dissolution time (MDT) vs mean residence time (MRT) or mean absorption time (MAT) | Uses all data but not point-to-point; different profiles can give the same mean; not for regulatory waivers |
| C | One dissolution parameter (t50, % at 4 h) vs one PK parameter (AUC, Cmax) | Weakest; useful in early development |
| Multiple C | Several dissolution time points each vs one or more PK parameters | Can be as useful as Level A if it covers the profile |
| D | Rank order (qualitative) | Not a true correlation; development aid only |

### Developing a Level A correlation

1. Make at least two, preferably three, formulations with different release rates (slow, medium, fast).
2. Obtain dissolution profiles with a discriminating method.
3. Give each formulation (and usually an IV solution or immediate-release reference) to the same subjects and measure plasma profiles.
4. Find the in vivo fraction absorbed over time by **deconvolution**: Wagner–Nelson (one-compartment drugs), Loo–Riegelman (two-compartment) or numerical deconvolution using the unit impulse response (Unit 3).
5. Plot fraction absorbed vs fraction dissolved, fit the relationship (linear; time scaling or shifting if needed).
6. **Validate predictability:** use the model to predict Cmax and AUC by convolution. Internal predictability (formulations used to build the model): mean absolute prediction error (%PE) of 10% or less, and no single formulation above 15%. External predictability uses a new formulation.

%PE = [(observed − predicted)/observed] × 100

### Worked example 1 — Level A correlation (example numbers)

| Time (h) | Fraction dissolved (FD) | Fraction absorbed (FA, by Wagner–Nelson) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 0.15 | 0.12 |
| 2 | 0.32 | 0.30 |
| 4 | 0.50 | 0.47 |
| 6 | 0.66 | 0.65 |
| 8 | 0.80 | 0.78 |
| 12 | 0.92 | 0.90 |

Linear regression of FA on FD gives slope = 1.013, intercept = −0.029, r = 0.9998. Slope near 1 and intercept near 0 mean in vitro dissolution matches in vivo absorption almost 1:1, so the method is predictive.

If the observed Cmax of a validation batch is 11.5 mg/L and the model predicts 10.9 mg/L, %PE = (11.5 − 10.9)/11.5 × 100 = **5.2%**, within the 10% limit.

### Uses of a validated IVIVC

- Biowaiver for certain manufacturing changes (site, equipment, process, minor composition changes) without a new bioequivalence study.
- Setting clinically relevant dissolution specifications (the range at each time point linked to acceptable Cmax and AUC).
- Reducing human studies during development.

**When IVIVC is likely:** dissolution is rate-limiting (BCS II), extended-release products. **Unlikely:** permeability-limited drugs (BCS III), drugs with saturable absorption or variable first pass, very rapidly dissolving immediate-release products (dissolution not limiting).

## 2.9 Dissolution profile comparisons

Used for post-approval changes, comparing a test product with a reference, comparing strengths, and supporting biowaivers.

### Model-independent: difference factor f1 and similarity factor f2 (Moore and Flanner)

f1 = {Σ|Rt − Tt| / Σ Rt} × 100

f2 = 50 × log { [1 + (1/n) Σ (Rt − Tt)²]^(−0.5) × 100 }

where Rt and Tt are mean % dissolved of reference and test at time t, and n the number of time points.

- **f1 of 0–15 and f2 of 50–100** indicate similar profiles; f2 = 100 when profiles are identical; f2 = 50 corresponds to an average difference of about 10% at every point.
- Conditions: 12 units of each product; same test conditions; at least three time points (excluding zero); only **one** point after 85% dissolution of either product (EU guidance: up to the first point where either product reaches 85%); coefficient of variation not more than 20% at early points (for example 10–15 min) and not more than 10% at later points.
- If both products dissolve 85% or more within 15 min, the profiles are accepted as similar without f2.
- If variability is too high for f2, use multivariate statistical distance or bootstrap f2.

### Worked example 2 — f1 and f2 (example numbers)

| Time (min) | Reference R (%) | Test 1 T (%) | R − T | (R − T)² |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 42 | 36 | 6 | 36 |
| 15 | 58 | 51 | 7 | 49 |
| 20 | 71 | 65 | 6 | 36 |
| 30 | 86 | 82 | 4 | 16 |
| Sum | 257 | | 23 | 137 |

- f1 = 23/257 × 100 = **8.9** (within 0–15).
- f2 = 50 × log[100/√(1 + 137/4)] = 50 × log(100/5.937) = 50 × 1.226 = **61.3** → similar.

A second test product dissolving 25, 38, 52 and 70% at the same times gives differences 17, 20, 19, 16 (sum of squares 1306): f1 = 28.0 and f2 = 50 × log(100/√327.5) = **37.1** → not similar.

### Model-dependent and other approaches

- Fit a model (Weibull, first order, Korsmeyer–Peppas) to each profile and compare parameters with confidence regions.
- **Mean dissolution time (MDT)** and **dissolution efficiency (DE)** summarise a profile in one number.

MDT = Σ (tmid × ΔM) / Σ ΔM     DE = [AUC of the dissolution curve from 0 to t / (100% × t)] × 100

### Worked example 3 — MDT and DE (example numbers)

Reference profile: 0, 42, 58, 71, 86, 94% at 0, 10, 15, 20, 30, 45 min.

| Interval (min) | tmid | ΔM (%) | tmid × ΔM |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0–10 | 5.0 | 42 | 210.0 |
| 10–15 | 12.5 | 16 | 200.0 |
| 15–20 | 17.5 | 13 | 227.5 |
| 20–30 | 25.0 | 15 | 375.0 |
| 30–45 | 37.5 | 8 | 300.0 |
| Sum | | 94 | 1312.5 |

MDT = 1312.5/94 = **14.0 min**. Area under the dissolution curve (trapezoidal) = 2917.5 %·min, so DE(45 min) = 2917.5/(100 × 45) × 100 = **64.8%**.

## 2.10 Drug product stability and performance

Stability is part of performance: a product that dissolves well at release but slowly after six months is not a good product.

- **Physical changes:** polymorphic conversion, recrystallisation of amorphous drug, moisture uptake, tablet hardening, gelatin cross-linking, film-coat curing changes in extended-release products.
- **Chemical changes:** degradation of drug; degradants may be toxic.
- **Stability testing (ICH Q1A(R2)):** long-term, intermediate and accelerated conditions; accelerated is 40 °C/75% RH for 6 months. India is treated as climatic zone IVb (hot and very humid), so CDSCO expects long-term studies at 30 °C/75% RH. Dissolution is a stability-indicating test for solid oral products; packaging (blister material, desiccant) is chosen to protect performance.
- **In-use and photostability** where relevant (ICH Q1B).

## 2.11 Considerations in the design of a drug product

A systematic design starts from the patient and works back to the formulation:

1. **Pharmacodynamic and pharmacokinetic considerations:** therapeutic window, half-life, need for rapid onset or prolonged action, first-pass metabolism (may favour sublingual, transdermal or parenteral routes), variability.
2. **Drug substance properties:** solubility, permeability (BCS class), stability, particle and solid-state properties, dose.
3. **Route and dosage form:** patient age (paediatric liquids, orally disintegrating tablets for the elderly), compliance (once-daily extended release), local vs systemic effect.
4. **Bioavailability targets:** need for solubility enhancement for BCS II and IV; need for enteric protection; food effect.
5. **Manufacturability and cost:** robust process, scale-up, stability, packaging.
6. **Quality by design (ICH Q8–Q10):** define the quality target product profile (QTPP), identify critical quality attributes (CQAs, such as dissolution and assay), link them to critical material attributes and critical process parameters by risk assessment and design of experiments, set a design space and a control strategy.
7. **Regulatory strategy:** bioequivalence or biowaiver route for generics, IVIVC for extended-release products.

```text
 QTPP ─► CQAs (dissolution, assay, impurities) ─► risk assessment
     ─► DoE on material attributes and process parameters ─► design space
     ─► control strategy (specifications, in-process controls) ─► lifecycle management
```

## Remember

- Rate-limiting step decides which formulation change matters: dissolution-limited (BCS II) vs permeation-limited (BCS III).
- Dose number D0 = (dose/250)/Cs; above 1 means solubility-limited risk.
- USP apparatus 1 basket, 2 paddle, 3 reciprocating cylinder, 4 flow-through cell, 5 paddle over disc, 6 rotating cylinder, 7 reciprocating holder; 37 ± 0.5 °C, 900 mL, pH 1.2/4.5/6.8.
- S1: each ≥ Q + 5%; S2: mean of 12 ≥ Q, none < Q − 15%; S3: mean of 24 ≥ Q, ≤ 2 below Q − 15%, none below Q − 25%.
- IVIVC Level A point-to-point (best), B MDT vs MRT, C single point; validation %PE ≤ 10% average, ≤ 15% each.
- f1 0–15, f2 50–100 = similar; 12 units, ≥ 3 points, one point after 85%; no f2 needed if both ≥ 85% in 15 min.
- MDT = Σ tmid ΔM / Σ ΔM; DE = area under dissolution curve / (100 × t).
- Korsmeyer–Peppas n (slab): 0.5 Fickian, 0.5–1 anomalous, 1 Case II.
- India = zone IVb: long-term 30 °C/75% RH; accelerated 40 °C/75% RH.
